topics.topic: Atomic ordering between request admission or refresh and owner-session expiry
questions: What happens when a request passes the session check but the expiry pass acquires the required lock first and removes that session before the request acquires it?
What single ordering point decides whether an arriving request refreshes the idle limit before the expiry pass ends the session, and under what lock or atomic operation is last_request updated?

How is admission made atomic with the expiry pass, given that a request may pass the session check before taking the session lock and the pass may then remove the session, confirmation, or uploaded file before that admitted request uses them?

judgement.why: The unchanged passages and question are the same as P1: admission and idle renewal are decided at arrival, and an admitted request completes despite later expiry.

precedent.topic: Atomic ordering of last-request updates against session expiry
quotes:
An owner
   request is any request to the owner interface that
   carries the valid session, whatever its answer; its arrival restarts the 30
   minutes — of concurrent requests the latest arrival counts; before the
   first request it runs from the sign-in.

Validity is
   checked when a request arrives (A04 rule 6, stage 1); a request that
   passes it completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs, and
   a restart that interrupts it leaves nothing of it (A04 rule 4).
precedent.why: Validity and idle renewal are explicitly decided at request arrival, so a request arriving before the limit remains admitted even if a sweep later obtains the lock.

topics.topic: Backup audit-sequence meaning and empty-log value
questions: What value is recorded and what check passes when the store has never written an audit entry?
What value is recorded and what check is performed when the store has never written an audit entry and its audit log is empty?
Is the recorded number the persistent highest-ever sequence counter or the greatest surviving AuditEntry sequence, and what value represents a new store with no audit entries?

quotes:
It
   records, readable without its key, its instant, the release that made it,
   the last audit sequence number it holds and a digest of the key it was
   made with (never the key); its age is counted from that instant.

Second, it
   writes the backup under a temporary name and checks it: it decrypts it
   into a second temporary file, opens that for reading only, checks that it
   is the store version of its release, that the full integrity check (A17
   rule 5)
   passes and that its audit log ends at the recorded sequence number, and
   removes it;

Sequence numbers are never reused within a store's history (M09): changes
   that write an entry are applied one at a time, and each entry takes the
   number after the last that history ever wrote, kept in the store apart
   from the entries, so an erasure does not lower it.
judgement.divergence: One implementation records an explicit empty-log value such as zero and accepts a new-store backup when the empty log matches it; another requires an AuditEntry to supply an ending sequence and fails or omits that backup, which the owner notices through whether a kept backup and newest-backup instant exist.
judgement.why: The backup rule requires a recorded ending sequence and a matching check but never defines their behavior for an empty audit log.

topics.topic: Backup filename formats, timestamps, temporary names, and collision handling
questions: What are the exact name formats and timestamp precision, how is a unique temporary name chosen, and what happens if a pre-existing file, link or directory occupies that temporary name?
What are the exact prefixes and the canonical conversion of an instant into a kept filename, including precision, timezone notation and collision behavior for equal instants?
What are the two prefixes, the kept-name timestamp representation and precision, and the exact serialized layout and versioning of the unencrypted record and encrypted payload?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about backup filename grammar, timestamp encoding, temporary names and collisions was already assigned to State 6 by P20.

precedent.topic: Backup filename grammar, uniqueness, and existing-name collision handling
quotes:
Kept and temporary names begin with two different prefixes the release
   declares, neither beginning with the other;

A kept
   name is made from the backup's instant and is never overwritten: a backup
   whose kept name exists, or whose rename fails, is deleted and the run
   fails.
precedent.why: The prefixes, timestamp encoding and filename grammar are backup-format encodings owned by State 6; the texts already state that an existing kept name makes the new run fail without overwriting it.

topics.topic: Configuration value syntax, encoding, secret decoding, length, and equality
questions: What makes each configuration value well formed beyond presence and secret length, including the accepted text encoding and representation of paths, credentials, tokens and the backup key?
How are environment-variable text values converted to bytes for length, constant-time comparison and equality, and are Unicode normalization or alternate encodings significant?
How is the byte length of an environment-variable value computed, and is the backup key an encoded random key, raw text used directly, or input to a key-derivation function?
What encodings and grammars make paths, tokens, the owner credential, and the backup key well formed, and are the 32 bytes counted before or after decoding an environment-variable string?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about configuration syntax, encoding, decoding and secret byte measurement is the same as P23.

precedent.topic: Configuration value syntax, encoding, and secret byte representation or length measurement
quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
precedent.why: The textual or binary representation, decoding, equality and byte-counting rules for credential fields are encoding and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Encrypted-backup cryptographic construction and file framing
questions: Which authenticated-encryption algorithm, nonce-generation rule and key-derivation rule are required, especially since A17 accepts secrets of any length of at least 32 bytes?
Which authenticated-encryption construction, nonce generation, key interpretation or derivation, file format, and key-digest algorithm must implementations use?
Which authenticated-encryption algorithm, nonce generation rule, key size and encoding, file framing, associated data, and authentication-failure behavior define an encrypted backup?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about authenticated encryption, nonce rules, key interpretation and backup framing is the same as P13.

precedent.topic: Authenticated backup encryption format, nonce rules, and key identification
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Exact environment-variable names for configuration fields
questions: What is the exact environment-variable name for each store location, backup location, backup key, owner credential and service token?
What are the exact REGISTRY_ variable names and the accepted representation and syntax of the store location, backup location, backup key, owner credential and service tokens?
What is the exact environment-variable name for each listed item, including each of the four service tokens?

judgement.why: The unchanged question asks for the exact configuration environment-variable names already assigned to State 6 by P24.

quotes:
The configuration is the set of environment variables whose names begin
   with `REGISTRY_`, set as R0-23 says; no other variable is read or
   checked. It holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 9).
precedent.why: Exact environment-variable names are configuration field names and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Expiry-pass startup timing, cadence, and overrun behavior
questions: Does the first pass run at startup or 60 seconds later, and when a pass lasts longer than 60 seconds are later passes skipped, coalesced, queued or overlapped?

If a pass lasts longer than 60 seconds, does Registry overlap passes, skip elapsed ticks, or start another pass immediately afterward; and is the import lock held once for the whole pass or reacquired for each session?
Does the first expiry pass run at instance start or 60 seconds later, and are later passes fixed to the start-time cadence or scheduled 60 seconds after the previous pass finishes?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about the expiry pass's first run, cadence, delay and overlap is the same as P15; its lock-scope variant is likewise non-observable because request validity is determined independently at arrival.

precedent.topic: Cleanup-pass first-run, cadence, delay, overlap, and catch-up rules
quotes:
Registry
   ends it — and drops its pending confirmation and its uploaded file with it
   (M11) — at a pass over the sessions it makes every 60 seconds from the
   start; the pass alone ends sessions by their limits, taking the import
   lock and then each session's lock (A16 rule 2) and deciding under them.

A session that has reached a limit serves no request from that
   moment: a request carrying it is refused at the session check.
precedent.why: The limits themselves determine request refusal exactly, so the first tick, delayed-tick policy and overlap handling affect only internal reclamation of already inaccessible session state.

topics.topic: Locks required when an accepted import clears other sessions' uploads
questions: May an accepted import drop uploads from other sessions while holding only the import lock, or must it also acquire each affected session's lock, and if so in what scope?

May the confirming request mutate uploads in other sessions while holding only the import lock and its own session lock, or must it also take every affected session's lock; if it must, in what order are those locks acquired?
Must an accepted import take every affected session's lock before dropping that session's upload, or is the import lock alone authoritative for uploaded-file state despite the session-lock rule?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about whether an accepted import also takes other sessions' locks while clearing uploads is the same as P28.

precedent.topic: Locking required when an accepted import drops uploads in other sessions
quotes:
Uploads
   and every other request that reads or changes an uploaded file — showing
   the mapping or the import's confirmation step, confirming, a sign-out —
   take the instance's one import lock first, then their session's lock
   (A13), check the closure while holding them, and hold both until done;

An uploaded file is changed only by a holder of the import lock: an
   accepted import, holding it, drops every session's upload; the upload of
   a session ended by its limits goes with the session, when Registry ends it
   (A13 rule 2).
precedent.why: The import lock already excludes every other operation that can read or change an upload, so additionally taking the other sessions' locks changes only internal waiting and not any specified result.

topics.topic: Visibility, format, authentication, and key-digest verification of backup metadata
questions: Is the unencrypted record authenticated, what exact format and version does it use, and which digest algorithm and encoding identify the backup key?
Does the no-key readability prohibition cover the whole backup file, or only its encrypted store payload while the listed metadata remains readable?
Must the unencrypted instant, release, key digest and sequence metadata be cryptographically authenticated and cross-checked with values inside the decrypted backup?
Which digest algorithm and byte representation are used, and is the recorded digest verified against the configured key during the make-and-check run?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about readable backup metadata, its authentication and the key-digest construction is the same as P2.

precedent.topic: Authentication of readable backup metadata and key-digest construction
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Clock semantics for owner-session time limits
questions: Which clock measures the 8-hour, 30-minute, 10-minute, 15-minute and 60-second intervals, and what happens when the system wall clock moves forward or backward?
Are these durations measured with the UTC wall clock or a monotonic elapsed-time clock, and what happens when the system clock moves backward or forward?

quotes:
The session ends at the first of: 8 hours after sign-in; 30 minutes without
   an owner request; the owner's sign-out; the instance's restart (M11 is never
   durable).

Registry
   ends it — and drops its pending confirmation and its uploaded file with it
   (M11) — at a pass over the sessions it makes every 60 seconds from the
   start; the pass alone ends sessions by their limits, taking the import
   lock and then each session's lock (A16 rule 2) and deciding under them.

It is valid only in that session, while
   less than 10 minutes have passed since it was shown, and is used up by the first submission that carries it, whatever
   its answer; a refused submission needs the step shown again.

Registry counts the sign-ins refused for a wrong or missing credential
   whose instant is less than 15 minutes before now, for the whole instance:
   Registry tells no callers apart by address (R0-27).
judgement.divergence: One implementation measures elapsed limits with a monotonic clock, so wall-clock adjustments do not change session, confirmation or lockout lifetimes; another compares UTC wall-clock instants, so a forward or backward adjustment expires or prolongs them, which the owner notices through accepted or refused requests and sign-ins.
judgement.why: The texts set several elapsed-time rules but do not choose the clock or define behavior when the wall clock changes.

topics.topic: Expiry-pass traversal, lock scope, and expiry-test timing
questions: Does one pass hold the import lock for the entire traversal, and does it acquire and release each session lock separately or hold all session locks together?

Which sessions belong to a pass, is the import lock held for the whole pass or reacquired for each session, and is expiry tested against one pass-start instant or the instant each session lock is acquired?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about expiry-pass membership, import-lock scope, per-session locking and test timing is the same as P21.

precedent.topic: Expiry-pass import-lock scope and iteration membership
quotes:
Registry
   ends it — and drops its pending confirmation and its uploaded file with it
   (M11) — at a pass over the sessions it makes every 60 seconds from the
   start; the pass alone ends sessions by their limits, taking the import
   lock and then each session's lock (A16 rule 2) and deciding under them.

A session that has reached a limit serves no request from that
   moment: a request carrying it is refused at the session check.
precedent.why: Holding the import lock for the whole visit or per session, and snapshotting or dynamically enumerating sessions, changes only internal waiting and reclamation because validity is decided from the fixed limits at request arrival.

topics.topic: Resolution and canonicalization of relative configuration paths
questions: Are relative store or backup paths accepted, and if they are, relative to which stable directory are they made absolute?
Are relative store or backup paths accepted, and if so, against which stable directory are they made absolute?

quotes:
The store and the
   backup location are different places, neither inside the other, compared
   by their absolute paths with every symbolic link resolved — for a store
   file that does not exist yet, its directory resolved and its name added; a
   path that cannot be resolved, a broken link or a loop included, fails the
   start; a configuration
   where they are the same or one holds the other fails the start.
judgement.why: Whether relative path strings are accepted and the base used to interpret them are configuration-field syntax and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Semantic validity rules for backup records and metadata
questions: What values count as readable and valid—for example, may the instant be in the future, the sequence be negative or exceed the store's counter, the release be unknown, or the key digest have an unexpected length?
Does ‘can all be read’ require only syntactic decoding, or also valid ranges, a known release, a non-future instant, a correctly sized digest, and consistency between the record and ciphertext?

judgement.why: The unchanged question about syntactic and semantic validation of readable backup metadata is the same as P14.

precedent.topic: Authentication and semantic validation of cleartext backup metadata
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Temporary new-store filename suffix, path derivation, and collision handling
questions: What suffix is declared, and what exact path results for store names with extensions or unusual filesystem characters?
What suffix does the release declare, how is collision with an existing non-temporary file prevented, and where is that declaration recorded for later implementations?

quotes:
When the store's
   configured file does not exist and its directory does, Registry makes a new,
   empty store of the running release's version there at the start, under a
   temporary name — the store's name with a suffix the release declares —
   that it renames to the store's name only once the store is complete;
judgement.why: The suffix, filename derivation and representation of the temporary store path are filename-format and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Exclusive ownership of shared store and backup locations by a Registry process
questions: What prevents two Registry processes using the same configuration from concurrently creating or opening the store and running backups in the same location?

topics.topic: Shutdown behavior while a backup run is active
questions: When Registry is asked to stop while a run is active, does shutdown wait for the run, cancel it and leave temporary files, or allow the run to finish independently?

topics.topic: Timing and failure semantics for clearing uploads after an accepted import
questions: At what point relative to the durable import transaction are all in-memory uploads dropped, and must they remain intact if the transaction fails?

topics.topic: Validation precedence and file-reading behavior when import is closed
questions: When the import is already closed and an upload is also oversized, unreadable, or malformed, which refusal wins, and may Registry parse or read the file before checking closure?
